questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Group B streptococcus

 

The CAMP test is a diagnostic test used to identify Group B Streptococcus (GBS), particularly Streptococcus agalactiae.

  • The test is based on the synergistic hemolysis between: β-lysin produced by Staphylococcus aureus, and CAMP factor produced by Group B Streptococcus
  • When GBS is streaked perpendicular to a streak of S. aureus on blood agar, a characteristic arrowhead-shaped zone of enhanced hemolysis appears near the junction giving it a CAMP-positive reaction.
    Other organisms giving positive CAMP test is Listeria monocytogenes. 
     

 

Educational Objective: 

 

CAMP test is positive for Group B Streptococcus (S. agalactiae), showing characteristic arrowhead-shaped enhanced hemolysis when grown perpendicular to S. aureus due to synergy between CAMP factor and beta-lysin. Remember: "CAMP = Christie, Atkins, Munch-Petersen (discoverers) = Group B" - also positive in Listeria monocytogenes.

questions.stem: Causative agent of acute rheumatic fever:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Group-A β-hemolytic streptococcus

 

The causative agent of acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus, specifically Streptococcus pyogenes.

  • ARF is a post-streptococcal autoimmune complication that follows an untreated or inadequately treated pharyngeal infection with S. pyogenes.
  • The body forms antibodies against streptococcal M proteins, which cross-react with human tissues (molecular mimicry), especially in the heart, joints, skin, and brain.
     

Other Options:

 

Option B. Group-B β -hemolytic streptococcus: also called as Streptococcus. Agalactiae, it causes neonatal infections

 

Option C & Option D. Group-C & Dβ -hemolytic streptococcus: Mostly cause infections in animals or other conditions like endocarditis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Acute rheumatic fever is caused by Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) following untreated pharyngitis, where antibodies against streptococcal M protein cross-react with human tissues (molecular mimicry) affecting heart, joints, brain, and skin. Remember: "Group A = Acute rheumatic fever" - only pharyngeal (not skin) infections trigger ARF.

questions.stem: A patient admitted to an ICU is on central venous line for the last one week. He is on ceftazidime and amikacin. After 7 days of antibiotics, he develops a spike of fever and his blood culture is positive for Gram-positive cocci in chains, which are catalase negative. Following this, vancomycin was started but the culture remained positive for the same organism even after 2 weeks of therapy. The most likely organism causing infection is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. Enterococcus faecalis 

 

This is a classic case of nosocomial bloodstream infection in an ICU patient with a central venous catheter.

 

Gram-positive cocci in pairs/chains → Suggests Streptococcus or Enterococcus (not Staphylococcus, which appears in clusters)
 

Catalase negative → Confirms not Staphylococcus which is catalase positive 
Persistently positive blood cultures despite vancomycin → Suggests intrinsically resistant organism or vancomycin tolerance
 

On ceftazidime and amikacin → These antibiotics do not cover Enterococcus well, which can persist
 

Other Options:
 

Option A. Staphylococcus aureus → Catalase positive and forms gram positive cocci in clusters
 

Option B. Viridans streptococci → gram positive cocci in chains not pairs and usually sensitive to vancomycin, not as persistent
 

Option D. Coagulase-negative staphylococcus → coagulase negative, Catalase positive and forms  gram positive cocci in clusters just like staphylococcus aureus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

ICU patient with central line infection showing catalase-negative, gram-positive cocci in pairs that persist despite vancomycin points to Enterococcus faecalis - known for intrinsic vancomycin resistance/tolerance and catheter-related infections. Remember: "Enterococcus = Enters ICU, Endures vancomycin" - catalase-negative rules out all staphylococci.

questions.stem: Heating at 60°C for 30 minutes would isolate:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B. Enterococci

 

Enterococci are more heat-resistant than most other non-spore-forming Gram-positive cocci.
 

Enterococcus spp. (e.g., E. faecalis) can survive heating at 60°C for 30 minutes, a property that helps differentiate them from Streptococci (which are more heat-labile).
 

This method called as the Heat Test, is often used to selectively isolate Enterococci from fecal samples or mixed cultures in bile esculin agar with heat treatment.
 

Other options:

 

Option A. Staphylococci: can tolerate heat to some extent, they do not reliably survive the standard 60°C for 30 minutes used in the Enterococcus isolation protocol.

 

Option C. Micrococci: they do not survive the standard 60°C for 30 minutes, they are killed
 

Option D. Streptococci: they do not survive the standard 60°C for 30 minutes, they are killed

 

Educational Objective:

 

Enterococci uniquely survive heating at 60°C for 30 minutes among non-spore-forming gram-positive cocci, making this heat test a selective isolation method that kills streptococci, staphylococci, and micrococci while preserving enterococci. Remember: "Enterococci are tough - Endure heat, Enter gut, Endure antibiotics."

questions.stem: A patient of RHD developed infective endocarditis after dental extraction. Most likely organism causing this is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A. Streptococcus viridans

 

Patients with Rheumatic Heart Disease (RHD) have damaged heart valves, making them more susceptible to infective endocarditis, especially after procedures like dental extraction.
 

Viridans streptococci group are:
 

Part of the normal oral flora and commonly enter the bloodstream during dental procedures
 

The most common cause of subacute infective endocarditis, especially in patients with preexisting valvular disease like RHD

 

Other options: 
 

Options B. Streptococcus pneumoniae – Causes pneumonia, otitis, meningitis; not typical in endocarditis post-dental work.
 

Options C. Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A) – Associated with pharyngitis , Rheumatic fever and skin infections; rare cause of endocarditis.
 

Options D. Staphylococcus aureus – More common in acute endocarditis, especially in IV drug users or native valves.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Viridans streptococci from normal oral flora are the most common cause of infective endocarditis following dental procedures in patients with pre-existing valvular disease like RHD, causing subacute infection on damaged valves. Remember: "Viridans = Vegetation on Valves after Dental work" - this is why antibiotic prophylaxis is crucial in high-risk cardiac patients.

questions.stem: A person presents with pneumonia. His sputum wassent for culture. The bacterium obtained was gram positive cocci in chains and alpha haemolytic colonies on sheep agar. Which of the following will help in. confirming the diagnosis:
Staphylococcus aureus differs from Staphylococcus epidermidis by:

options.label: B
options.text: Forming yellow colonies on media due to pigment production

options.label: C
options.text: Being a common cause of early prosthetic valve endocarditis

questions.answerText: Being a common cause of early prosthetic valve endocarditis
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C. being a common cause of early prosthetic valve endocarditis

 

Staphylococcus epidermidis is a coagulae negative staphylococcus species(CoNS) that causes early prosthetic valve endocarditis which occurs within 1 year of prosthetic valve replacement. 

It differs from staphylococcus by being coagulase negative, showing white colonies on media and by causing prosthetic wall endocarditis.

 

Other options:

 

Option A. Is coagulase positive: Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase positive while staphylococcus epidermidis is coagulase negative hence differentiating the two organism.

 

Option B. Forming yellow colonies on media due to pigment production: Staphylococcus aureus produces yellow colonies on culture media due to the pigment 9 beta carotene) production. While staphylococcus epidermidis produces white colonies on culture media.

 

Option D.  Causing endocarditis in drug addicts: Staphylococcus aureus is known to cause native valve endocarditis in IV drug users.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

S. epidermidis is the most common cause of early prosthetic valve endocarditis (within 1 year), making this a similarity NOT a difference from S. aureus which also causes prosthetic valve infections. The key differences are: S. aureus is coagulase-positive with golden colonies and causes acute native valve endocarditis, while S. epidermidis is coagulase-negative with white colonies.

questions.stemHtml: 15 A 9-years old child presented to OPD with complaints of high-grade fever, vomiting, one episode of seizure. CSF examination was done and Gram staining of the culture showed the following finding. What is the probable causative agent?
questions.solutionHtml: Ans. C. Streptococcus pneumonia

Ans. C. Staphylococcus saprophyticus

 

Catalase positive novobiocin-resistant bacteria:
 

Catalase positive means the bacteria produce the enzyme catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide.


Novobiocin resistance means the bacteria are resistant to the antibiotic novobiocin.
 

Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a catalase positive, coagulae negative, novobiocin resistant organism that causes urinary tract infections in reproductive age females.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Staphylococcus aureus; it is Catalase positive, but novobiocin sensitive

 

Option B. Staphylococcus epidermidis: Catalase positive, novobiocin sensitive.

 

Educational Objective: 

 

Among staphylococci, S. saprophyticus is uniquely novobiocin-resistant while still being catalase-positive, distinguishing it from other coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis is novobiocin-sensitive). Remember: "Saprophyticus is Stubborn (resistant)" - important for identifying this common UTI pathogen in young women.

questions.stem: Mannitol salt agar is used for isolation of:
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is caused by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. Epidermolytic toxin

 

Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) is caused by the release of epidermolytic toxins (also known as exfoliative toxins) produced by Staphylococcus aureus.
 

Epidermolytic toxins (Exfoliative toxins) target desmoglein-1, a protein involved in cell-to-cell adhesion in the skin. 

 

This leads to blistering and peeling of the skin, characteristic of SSSS.

 

These toxins are heat-labile, meaning they are sensitive to heat and are superantigens. 
 

Other Options: 
 

Option A. Hemolysin – Causes red blood cell lysis but not the blistering seen in SSSS
 

Option  B. Coagulase – An enzyme that clots plasma; involved in virulence but not in SSSS
 

Option C. Enterotoxin – Causes food poisoning symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea) but not SSSS

 

Educational Objective:

 

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) is caused by epidermolytic/exfoliative toxins from S. aureus that cleave desmoglein-1, causing superficial skin blistering and peeling that resembles a burn. Remember: "Epidermolytic = Epidermis splits" - these toxins act as "molecular scissors" cutting skin cell connections.
